scores.position: STAY on Next.js/TypeScript and pay down the confirmed debt with a scoped, shippable refactor.
scores.strengths: Its central claim survives inspection. I read every high-severity finding title across the four assessments: scheduler self-disable, no migration ledger, usage cron with no maxDuration, ship-skill checking the wrong host, CLAUDE.md's lint table being false, README describing a prototype, the Supabase driver untested, field-to-column maps unpinned, the ISR assumption, the 10s heartbeat, liveOnly. Not one is a language defect; every one reproduces in Go or Java on day one. I confirmed the two framework-specific findings independently: .eslintrc.json's overrides block (lines 25-29) exempts lib/env.ts, scripts, e2e and tests but never middleware.ts, while middleware.ts:23,34,74 carries four genuine process.env reads that `next lint` never visits — so `pnpm verify` is greener than the codebase, exactly as claimed. Every structural claim about the seams checks out: lib/catalogue-access.ts is 88 lines, lib/video/provider.ts is 151, middleware.ts is 122, lib/db/repository.ts is 404, 14 runtime dependencies, 24 migrations, 60 API routes. The line split that decides a backend port's scope is accurate to the line (app 8,270 + lib 10,952 + middleware 122 against components 13,326 + modules 2,213 + themes 382). The 49 real=true and 26 matters_next_12_months counts are exact (12+14+11+12 and 5+9+6+6). Crucially, the fix-speed argument is stronger than written: the liveOnly photo fix is not sitting uncommitted, it is HEAD (7730633, 16 Sept, clean tree). On the two axes that carry six of ten weight, nothing else is close — the first slice ships in week one and the cost of being wrong is one sprint.
scores.weaknesses: One load-bearing claim is simply false, and it is the one that does the rhetorical work: 'Exactly two are high severity and they are the same root cause.' There are twelve high-severity findings across assess-deployability (3), assess-documentation (3), assess-maintainability (2) and assess-scalability (4). The severity profile is six times worse than the position represents it, and the 46-of-49-are-neutral argument did not need the lie. Second, R3 (6 days, 'make the guest page actually cached') is work the codebase's own author already argued against on the merits: lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-17 states that /c/[slug] reads cookies() for locale, profile and passcode grant and that 'a page cached across guests could not answer' whether a guest may see it. Moving locale onto a header does not remove the conditional passcode-grant read, so the route stays dynamic for exactly the catalogues where caching would matter. Both rivals identify this correctly and STAY does not. Third, the position is honest that commerce is greenfield and that refactoring does not build it — but then spends four calendar months on debt anyway. A pre-revenue product with 6 orgs whose actual blocker is that no Razorpay code exists should not spend its next quarter on a debt sprint of which only about twelve days (R2, R6a, and the staging half of R5) are genuinely urgent. Fourth, it does nothing about the bus factor of one or the thin Next.js/RSC hiring pool, and its own summary overstates the fix-in-a-day story: the titles half of the same bug is still live at HEAD (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1390-1391 filters `published` and `status`, never live_at, against memory-repository.ts:747's explicit comment that liveAt is the gate).

scores.position: Port the backend to Go — one binary in two roles (api, worker) against the same Postgres, keeping React and Bunny, as a strangler with an explicit stop after the worker.
scores.strengths: The best-reasoned of the three documents and the only one that argues honestly against its own conclusion. Its diagnosis is the sharpest available: the repository does not feel unmanageable because it is large — 35k lines is small — it feels that way because the runtime is scattered across Vercel crons, GitHub Actions, PostgREST and per-process memory, and four of those four are confirmed. I verified vercel.json carries exactly two crons, notify-drain.yml's own header states a public repo's schedules disable after 60 days of no commits, ci.yml pins DATA_DRIVER=memory and VIDEO_DRIVER=fake for every job, lib/http/rate-limit.ts:1-12 confesses its own per-instance approximation, and grep for maxDuration across app/, lib/, next.config.ts and vercel.json returns zero. Its correction of the ISR claim is right and STAY's is wrong. The service-boundary reasoning is the best engineering in the pack — 'every service boundary you could draw here cuts through a transaction', with publish and handover named — and it correctly refuses both the six-service decomposition and the Vite SPA, keeping Next server-rendered for the 1.5s budget. The sqlc argument is the strongest technical case any position makes: generated-from-column mapping makes the drift class structurally impossible rather than merely tested against. And its single most valuable sentence is an argument against itself: about 80% of the port's value is banked in month 2 for 1.5 of 13 engineer-months.
scores.weaknesses: It costs 13 engineer-months and 8 calendar months at a company with 6 orgs, 5 catalogues, zero payment code and no invoice table — and by its own stop-trigger, Razorpay must be live by month 3, which means the two engineers are simultaneously at 81% on the port and shipping commerce and carrying 10 weddings/month of support. That arithmetic does not close. The velocity baseline is explicitly anomalous and the document says so: 179 commits in five weeks from one author plus an agent, with agent leverage weaker on a port than on greenfield because the correctness criterion is 'matches undocumented behaviour', so the 13 is a planning number with a self-declared 2x miss risk. It concedes the port touches none of the 13,326 React lines at 17% coverage, none of the fifteen documentation findings, and none of the commerce gap — that is most of what actually hurts. It concedes the hermetic 659-test suite is the real loss and that Docker becomes a precondition for running tests at all, against CLAUDE.md's explicit argument that a suite needing a database is a suite nobody runs. Its Zod double-duty tax is the correct diagnosis of the recurring cost and it is invisible in month 1. Its own risk list names the failure mode accurately: finishes in month 8 exactly where month 0 was, minus the Razorpay integration that would have made it a business. Minor: 'the Next server surface is 40 page files that fetch and compose' overstates — only 26 of 40 import the repository, so the rewire is smaller than claimed, but 'all 40 pages are server components (zero carry use client)' is exactly right.
scores.verdict_note: I score the whole position, not its month-2 step. The month-2 step is the best idea in the pack and I have grafted it.

scores.position: Port the backend to Java 21 / Spring Boot behind the existing React front end, keep Bunny, keep Postgres.
scores.strengths: The most intellectually honest document of the three about its own verdict — it states plainly that nobody should do this at 6 orgs and 5 catalogues pre-revenue, and that the sentence about the port producing more total lines in two languages should settle it if nothing else does. Its execution-model diagnosis is identical to Go's and equally correct. It is the only position that gets the page-composition number exactly right: I counted 26 of 40 page.tsx files importing the repository inside a server component, and it correctly names slice 4 as the one everyone underestimates and forces an explicit choice between BFF and client-rendering rather than letting it be decided implicitly. Its module-contract analysis is the best in the pack and the only one that names a genuine architectural regression the port causes: modules/billboard/index.ts holds schema, Guest, Editor, defaults, consumes and advise in one file, tests/unit/registry.test.ts enforces that nothing outside modules/ names a module type, and no test can span a Java/TypeScript boundary — so .claude/skills/add-module's one-folder premise dies. Its grant research is the only primary-source work anyone did, and its conclusion is blunt and correct: DPIIT recognition tests entity type, age, turnover and a self-certified innovation sentence; SISFS scores eight criteria set by the incubator; backend language appears in none of them, and a milestone-based disbursement cannot recognise an internal port. Its ArchUnit proposal for the org-scoping rule is a real improvement over STAY's tree-walking test — I confirmed the five guards in lib/admin/session.ts (getOperatorSession:17, getSessionOrg:49, requireOperator:53, requireOwnedCatalogue:69, requireEditableCatalogue:115) and that nothing enforces their use.
scores.weaknesses: 18 engineer-months, 11 calendar, with a self-declared honest range of 14–22 and the wide end 'more likely than the narrow one' — the longest and least reversible of the three, at the moment of maximum runway sensitivity. Its stated premise is a hire that has not happened: 'if the answer to am I hiring a backend engineer in the next two quarters is no or maybe, the correct decision is to not start.' That is a conditional, and the condition is currently false. Its headline defect claim is stale by one commit: it asserts listPhotosForCatalogue 'takes no options parameter at all' and that 'every photograph is guest-visible on upload, before Publish, in production, right now' — as of HEAD 7730633 the signature takes `options?: { liveOnly?: boolean }` and applies `.not('live_at','is',null)` at lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1641, with a comment naming the 15 September review. Its Month 0 first item is therefore already done. Its 'makes per-instance state global by construction' is overstated and it concedes the correction two clauses later: with two instances behind the load balancer its own cost line budgets for, it still needs Redis. Its infra figure of ₹23,300/month is ₹7,500 above Go's for a near-identical two-instance architecture, and the delta is mostly a log-retention line and a Redis line that Go omits rather than a JVM premium — both numbers are unquoted estimates presented with false precision. And its own risk list concedes a naive Spring port produces more code than the 10,952 lines of lib/ it replaces, which directly defeats the complaint that prompted the question. The hiring argument is real and is the only reason to prefer Java over Go, but it buys one point of weight-1 criterion for six weighted points of time-to-revenue and delivery risk.

winner: STAY on Next.js/TypeScript and pay down the confirmed debt with a scoped, shippable refactor.
rationale:
On the weighted criteria this is not close, and the decisive fact is one I verified rather than took on trust. I read the severity field of every finding in the four assessment files: twelve are high. Their titles are a scheduler that disables itself after 60 days, no migration ledger, a usage cron with no wall-clock bound, a deploy skill checking the wrong host, a lint config that never visits middleware.ts, a README describing a prototype, a production driver no test executes, field-to-column maps unpinned to the schema, a capacity plan built on ISR that does not exist, a 10-second heartbeat at 12x the modelled function budget, and the liveOnly divergence. Every single one is reproducible in Go or Java on day one, and the two ports would carry eleven of them across intact while spending 13 to 18 engineer-months. That is the whole argument, and it holds even though STAY misstated the count in its own favour.

The weights do the rest. Time-to-revenue (3) and 12-month delivery risk (3) are six of ten, and they point the same way: the refactor's first slice ships in week one and its cost-of-being-wrong is one sprint, against 8 to 11 calendar months in which no customer-visible thing ships at a pre-revenue company whose actual blocker is that `plans` is a table with zero rows and no reader and RAZORPAY appears nowhere in the repository. Both port documents concede this in their own words — Go's failure mode is 'finishes in month 8 exactly where month 0 was, minus the Razorpay integration that would have made the thing a business', and Java states outright that nobody should do this at 6 orgs pre-revenue. When both rival advocates argue their own case down, the judge should listen.

Maintainability at 3 years (2) is where the ports earn their points and I have given them: Go's sqlc argument is correct on the merits, one implementation against the real engine makes driver drift structurally impossible rather than merely tested against, and Java's ArchUnit enforcement of the org-scoping rule is genuinely stronger than a tree-walking test. Hiring (1) is Java's and I have given it that too — the Next.js App Router plus RSC plus hand-rolled repository pool in India is thin, and 179 commits from one author is a bus factor of one that STAY does nothing about. But grants (1) is a wash by Java's own primary-source research, and four weighted points cannot outrun six.

The honest qualification, which changes the shape of the win: STAY's plan is right in kind and too long in degree. About twelve days of it are urgent — the titles half of liveOnly (still live at supabase-repository.ts:1390-1391), `eslint .` replacing `next lint`, and a staging environment plus a platform scheduler. R3 should be deleted outright because the codebase already refuted it, and the remainder should be interleaved with commerce rather than sequenced ahead of it. What I am endorsing is the diagnosis and the first seven weeks, not a four-month debt quarter at a company with no payment code.
graft_from_losers: From Go, the single best idea in the pack and the one to execute first: its month-2 step, in TypeScript. Move all six jobs onto one platform scheduler and retire .github/workflows/notify-drain.yml and synthetic-check.yml, whose own header (lines 14-15) states that a public repository's schedules are disabled after 60 days with no commits — today that workflow drives lifecycle, warnings, notify and the hourly synthetic check, which is every alert path, and the alert about the failure is queued in the queue that stopped draining. Go prices this at 1.5 of its 13 engineer-months for 'about 80% of the port's value'. STAY buries it inside a 10-day R5 in weeks 2-3; it should be week one, ahead of everything except the titles fix.

From Go, the shadow-read as a cheaper substitute for half of STAY's R1. Before building a full conformance suite, run both drivers against the same reads and log divergence. It is the cheapest possible test of whether the seam is actually producing bugs, it would have caught live_at, and Go correctly makes it the go/no-go gate ('stop if the shadow-read finds fewer than about three real divergences'). STAY's R1 spends 10 days assuming the answer; the shadow-read buys the answer first.

From Go, the sqlc insight applied inside TypeScript: generated-from-the-column beats hand-written-and-tested. STAY already has `supabase gen types typescript` as a 2-day item inside R1; it should be lifted out and run before the conformance suite, because it closes the untested-field-map high-severity finding by construction rather than by assertion. This is the one place the rival case is right on the merits and it costs two days here instead of nine months there.

From Java, the ArchUnit-shaped enforcement of the org-scoping invariant, adapted. Java is right that STAY's proposed test is the weaker instrument and right about why: lib/admin/session.ts's five guards hold perfectly across 34 route files today with no automated check at all. Write it as a structural rule (every handler under app/api/admin must reach a guard on every path) rather than a grep for five function names — and write it from a read of the tree, since the verify pass already showed the naive version rejects 11 legitimate pages and misses that /admin/login, /register and /new are deliberately unauthenticated.

From Java, the Month 0 discipline: fix in TypeScript what is broken now, deliberately, before any larger decision, and budget it as throwaway if the decision later changes. STAY has the same items but frames them as slice one of a programme; Java's framing is better because it survives the programme being cancelled.

From Java, staging as a precondition rather than a line item. N-87 is the one piece of work that is valuable whichever of the three positions is right, and STAY buries it inside a 10-day R5. Today a migration and the build that needs it meet for the first time in production (docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:116 concedes there is no ledger; ci.yml pins DATA_DRIVER=memory for every job including E2E). Do it first and alone.

From Java, the decision rule STAY is missing entirely, which is the best single sentence in any of the three documents: start the port the week before a second backend engineer starts, and not before. STAY's triggers-to-revisit list six conditions and none of them is 'a second engineer was hired' — which is the actual trigger, because the port's entire remaining case is hiring pool and bus factor, and both are dormant at a team of one.

From both losers, the correction that deletes work from the winner: drop R3 (6 days) in full. lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-17 already argues that /c/[slug] cannot be statically cached because access depends on the passcode-grant cookie, and moving locale onto a header does not remove that conditional read. Go states the guest page 'is NOT ISR-cached today and cannot be'; Java states nothing static is being given up. Both are right and STAY is wrong. Spend those six days on Razorpay.

From Go, the framing to keep for the eventual scale conversation: if the two hot paths (progress heartbeat, playback-token mint) ever become binding, they are a separate service behind interfaces that already exist — lib/video/provider.ts's five methods and the Repository seam — not a reason to retype lib/catalogue-access.ts's 88 lines.
disbelieved: STAY: 'Two are high severity and they are the same root cause.' False, and it is the claim the position's rhetoric rests on. Counting the severity field directly: assess-deployability 3 high, assess-documentation 3, assess-maintainability 2, assess-scalability 4 — twelve, not two. The other ten are the 60-day scheduler self-disable, the absent migration ledger, the unbounded usage cron, the ship skill checking a host the backlog calls luck, CLAUDE.md's enforced-rules table being false for middleware.ts/modules/themes, README's 'Known gaps' describing a prototype, only 2 of ~20 field-to-column maps held to their schema, the capacity plan assuming an ISR that does not exist, and the 10-second heartbeat at ~12x the modelled function budget. The 46-of-49-are-language-neutral argument survives this correction intact, which is what makes the misstatement gratuitous.

STAY: 'as of 16 Sept the working tree carries M lib/db/supabase-repository.ts and an untracked tests/unit/supabase-query-shape.test.ts, both uncommitted on a clean-at-session-start main.' False. `git status` is clean and the change is HEAD — commit 7730633, 'Guests saw unpublished photographs on the Supabase driver', authored 16 Sept, with tests/unit/supabase-query-shape.test.ts present in tests/unit/. The substance favours STAY more than its own telling does, which makes the error odd rather than self-serving, but a diligence document should not be wrong about what is committed.

STAY: R3, 'Make the guest page actually cached' in 6 days. Disbelieved on the codebase's own reasoning. lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-17 is titled 'Why not static rendering' and states that /c/[slug] reads cookies() for the locale, the profile and the passcode grant, that this opts the route out of static generation, and that 'this is not a mistake to correct: whether a guest may see this catalogue depends on their cookies, and a page cached across guests could not answer it.' STAY's fix addresses locale (lib/guest-locale.ts:22-23, confirmed an unconditional cookies() call) and searchParams (app/c/[slug]/page.tsx:70, confirmed awaited) but leaves the passcode-grant read, so the route remains dynamic for precisely the catalogues where caching matters. Six days for a partial result the author already argued against.

STAY: 'A codebase where the worst bug in it is found and fixed in a day by one person and an agent is not unmanageable.' Half-true as stated. The photo half was fixed in a day; the titles half is still live at HEAD — lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1390-1391 gates publishedOnly on `.eq('published', true).eq('status','ready')` with no live_at predicate, against lib/db/memory-repository.ts:747's fourteen-line comment explaining that liveAt and not published is the guest gate, and against lib/schema.ts:461-464's own doc comment ('Null means the couple cannot see it, whatever published says'). STAY schedules this correctly as R2 day one; its summary should not have claimed the bug fixed.

JAVA: 'lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1625-1631 — listPhotosForCatalogue takes no options parameter at all… Every photograph is guest-visible on upload, before Publish, in production, right now.' False as of today. The method signature at :1624-1627 is `listPhotosForCatalogue(catalogueId: string, options?: { liveOnly?: boolean })` and :1641 applies `.not('live_at','is',null)`, under a comment naming the 15 September review and two reviewers. Java's Month 0 first action item is already complete. The titles half of its claim remains true.

JAVA: 'a JVM makes all three go away by construction' for per-process state. Overstated and self-contradicted. Its own cost line budgets two app instances plus a load balancer, and its own benefit text concedes 'with two instances behind a load balancer, one Redis line.' Two JVMs sharing nothing have the same per-instance rate-limit problem lib/http/rate-limit.ts:1-12 already documents. What the JVM removes is cold-start scatter, not the distributed-state requirement.

JAVA ₹23,300/month against GO ₹15,800/month for architectures that differ only in language. Both are unquoted estimates and neither is robust. The ₹7,500 delta is almost entirely Java's log-and-metric retention line (₹2,800) and Redis line (₹1,150) — costs Go's architecture also incurs and omits — plus a larger instance assumption. Java flags its own Mumbai instance prices as needing a quote before anyone commits; Go does not flag its. Treat both as ±40% and neither as a differentiator.

GO: 13 engineer-months over 8 calendar months for two people, while its own stop-trigger requires Razorpay and a working invoice live by month 3 and the business continues at 10 weddings/month of support. 13 engineer-months across 8 calendar months at two people is 81% allocation to the port alone; commerce and support are unfunded in that plan. Go also states agent leverage is materially weaker on a port than on greenfield and that planning at greenfield velocity misses by 2x. Its own honest floor is therefore closer to 8 calendar months at 100% allocation with no commerce, or ~12 with it — which is Java's range, not Go's.

GO and JAVA on component counts: Go's '64 of 70 components are client' and Java's '59 of 70 components already use client' are both loose on the denominator — 64 of 75 files under components/ carry 'use client'. Immaterial to either conclusion, but it is the kind of number a diligence reader spot-checks, and Go's numerator is right while Java's is not.

GO: 'the Next server surface is 40 page files that fetch and compose.' Only 26 of the 40 page.tsx files import the repository; the other 14 compose without a data read. The error is in Go's own disfavour — the rewire is smaller than it prices — and Java gets this number exactly right, which is a point in Java's favour on rigour even where its conclusion is weaker.

All three positions on transcoding, and here I disbelieve nothing — I checked because it is one of the five decisions on the table. cost.json is consistent across all three citations: Bunny ₹7,534/month at 10 weddings against ₹19,971 self-hosted infra-only and ₹54,971 with people (7.3x); ₹45,207 against ₹54,508/₹1,24,508 at 60; ₹2,26,034 against ₹2,49,416 at 300. No breakeven inside the modelled range once people are counted. All three positions keep Bunny and all three are right to. The in-house-transcoding question is settled and should be taken off the table, not re-litigated alongside the language question.
